strategy.angle: Hardware-Software Co-Design as a Competitive Moat

draft.hook: We are approaching a breaking point where your software strategy is entirely dictated by Taiwan's molten silicon manufacturing capacity.
draft.body: The pivot from simple LLMs to 'agentic AI' isn't a software upgrade; it’s a physical infrastructure overhaul. NVIDIA’s move to lock in the Vera Rubin platform via deep-integration manufacturing isn't just about speed—it's about hardware-software co-design. I’ve seen this before in Houston’s industrial sector: when you lose control of your physical supply chain, your competitive advantage vanishes. We are looking at a 40% increase in power-per-rack requirements to support these autonomous agents. Does this mean Houston businesses can no longer compete on AI? Not necessarily, but it means you must stop treating compute as a commodity cloud invoice and start treating it as a strategic supply chain asset. If your AI roadmap doesn't account for the physical scarcity of high-density compute, you aren't building a strategy; you’re buying a subscription to a bottleneck. At Amplify Intelligence, we tell our partners that the future of enterprise AI isn't just in the code repository—it's in the underlying silicon geography. As Leon Coe, I’ve watched many firms wait for 'better models' only to find they lack the underlying hardware density to run them reliably in production.
draft.closing: The infrastructure war determines who wins the enterprise AI race.
draft.cta: If you aren't auditing your hardware resilience, you're already behind. Are you building your AI stack on a foundation of shifting compute sand, or have you accounted for the physical realities of the Rubin era?
